content.title: Maintaining Clear Pronoun Referents and Information Flow
content.overview: This lesson focuses on ensuring every pronoun in a passage points clearly and logically to a single noun, known as its antecedent. On the ACT, you must identify and correct ambiguous pronouns that could refer to multiple nouns or that disrupt the logical flow of information.
learning_objectives: Identify ambiguous pronouns that lack a clear, single antecedent.
Apply the Signal-and-Name strategy to resolve pronoun confusion.
Select specific nouns to replace vague pronouns when multiple antecedents are present.
Organize sentence elements to ensure the referent immediately precedes the pronoun for better information flow.

sections.title: The Rule of Clear Antecedents
sections.content: A pronoun (like 'it,' 'they,' 'this,' or 'which') must refer to a specific noun that appeared earlier in the text. This noun is called the antecedent. For a sentence to be clear, the pronoun must match the antecedent in number (singular vs. plural) and gender. Most importantly, there should be no doubt which noun the pronoun is replacing. If a sentence contains two singular nouns and then uses 'it,' the reader may not know which noun is being discussed. This is called pronoun ambiguity.

sections.title: The Signal-and-Name Strategy
sections.content: When you encounter a pronoun-based question, use the Signal-and-Name method: 1. Signal: Locate the pronoun and underline all nearby nouns that could potentially be the antecedent. 2. Name: If the pronoun could logically refer to more than one of those nouns, replace the pronoun with the specific noun (the 'Name') to eliminate confusion. 3. Chain: Ensure the information flows logically by placing the referent as close to the pronoun as possible, ideally immediately preceding it.

sections.title: Information Flow and Proximity
sections.content: Information flow refers to the logical progression of ideas. A common ACT trap involves placing a pronoun too far from its antecedent or placing a different noun between them. To fix this, you may need to reorder the phrase so the intended referent is the last noun mentioned before the pronoun appears. If reordering doesn't work, the best solution is almost always to replace the pronoun with the specific noun it represents.

worked_examples.question:
Passage: During the gallery opening, the critic described the new installation as daring. After the review, it received many inquiries from collectors.

Which choice best clarifies the underlined word 'it'?
A. NO CHANGE
B. the review received many inquiries from collectors
C. the installation received many inquiries from collectors
D. the critic received many inquiries from collectors
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Locate the pronoun 'it'. Step 2: Identify possible antecedents. 'It' could refer to 'the installation' or 'the review'. Step 3: Evaluate logical focus. Collectors typically inquire about the art (the installation), not the written critique. Step 4: Replace the pronoun with the specific noun. Choice C clarifies that the installation is the object of interest. Choice B is a trap because while 'review' is closer to 'it', it makes less sense for collectors to inquire about a review. Correct Answer: C.

common_mistakes: Assuming the closest noun is always the antecedent: Sometimes a noun is physically close but logically incorrect.
Using 'this' or 'that' to refer to an entire previous idea: The ACT prefers a specific noun over a vague 'this' to start a sentence.
Ignoring number agreement: Using 'they' to refer to a singular company or 'it' to refer to a group of people.
exam_tips: If you see a pronoun underlined and the answer choices include specific nouns, the question is likely testing pronoun ambiguity.
The most specific answer is often the correct one if the original pronoun is even slightly vague.
Read the sentence with the noun replacement to ensure it doesn't sound redundant or change the intended meaning of the passage.
content.recap: To maintain clear information flow, ensure every pronoun has one unmistakable antecedent. When in doubt, replace a vague pronoun with a specific noun to remove ambiguity and keep the reader focused on the correct subject.

knowledge_claims.content: An antecedent is the specific noun that a pronoun replaces or refers back to in a sentence.
Pronoun ambiguity occurs when a single pronoun could logically refer to two or more different nouns mentioned previously.
The Signal-and-Name strategy involves underlining all possible antecedents and replacing a vague pronoun with the specific noun it represents.
A pronoun must match its antecedent in both number (singular/plural) and gender.
Information flow is maintained when the referent appears immediately before or within the same clause as the pronoun.
It is a mistake to use 'this' or 'that' to refer to a broad general concept or an entire preceding sentence without a clarifying noun.
To verify a pronoun's clarity, substitute the suspected noun into the pronoun's position and check if the sentence remains logically consistent.
When multiple singular nouns exist, replace the pronoun with the specific noun to ensure the reader knows which one is the subject.
Specific nouns are generally preferred over pronouns on the ACT English section if the pronoun's reference is even slightly unclear.
A 'jumpy' or disconnected sentence often indicates that the referent and pronoun are too far apart or separated by distracting nouns.
If reordering a sentence does not fix ambiguity, the most effective action is to name the antecedent directly.
Logical focus determines the correct antecedent when two nouns are grammatically possible but only one makes sense in context.

items.stem:
Practice form 1. Rina is editing a short report about a community garden.

Which revision makes the pronoun reference clearest?
A) When Maya met Priya, Maya explained the revised schedule.
B) When Maya met Priya, she explained it.
C) Meeting her, she explained the revised schedule.
D) Maya met Priya, and this explained that.

options.A: When Maya met Priya, Maya explained the revised schedule.
options.B: When Maya met Priya, she explained it.
options.C: Meeting her, she explained the revised schedule.
options.D: Maya met Priya, and this explained that.

items.explanation: The correct choice directly applies the target skill: 保持指代对象与信息链清晰.

videoLesson.title: Clarify Pronoun Referents for Smooth Flow
videoLesson.description: Recognize ambiguous pronouns and their nearest noun antecedents. Replace or name antecedents and reorder phrases so the referent immediately precedes the pronoun.
